{
  "research_question": "How do the five stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, Sham) differentially affect mouse navigation performance metrics (Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": [
    "Combined",
    "ICMS Only",
    "Dim Visual Only",
    "Bright Visual Only",
    "Sham"
  ],
  "response_variables": [
    "Time-to-Target",
    "Success",
    "Path Efficiency",
    "Average Speed",
    "AD"
  ],
  "anova_plan": [
    "Run a separate One-Way ANOVA for each of the five response variables: Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and AD, with Stim Paradigm as the fixed between-subjects factor.",
    "Hypothesis: Null hypothesis (H0) states that the mean performance for the metric is equal across all five stimulation paradigms (μ_Combined = μ_ICMS = μ_Dim = μ_Bright = μ_Sham). Alternative hypothesis (H1) states that at least one mean differs.",
    "Check homogeneity of variance (Levene's test) for each metric before proceeding, as sample sizes are unequal (Sham n=3505 vs Combined n=48846). If violated, use Welch's ANOVA.",
    "Analyze 'Success' separately as a binary metric (0/1) using a Chi-Square Test of Independence or one-way ANOVA if treated as continuous per dataset structure, though the binary nature suggests log-linear models might be stricter."
  ],
  "posthoc_plan": [
    "If global F-tests/P-values indicate significant differences, perform post-hoc pairwise comparisons for each metric.",
    "For continuous metrics (Time-to-Target, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, AD): Use Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test to compare all levels against each other to control family-wise error rate.",
    "For the binary metric (Success): If using ANOVA framework, report pairwise comparisons; ideally, convert to proportions and use Chi-Square tests or pairwise Benjamini-Hochberg corrected proportions tests.",
    "Focus interpretation on the large effect size likely present between 'Sham' and other groups based on summary means."
  ],
  "multiple_comparison_strategy": "Apply the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction (Benjamini-Hochberg procedure) across the set of all p-values derived from the five ANOVAs and subsequent post-hoc pairwise tests. This controls the expected proportion of false discoveries given the large number of comparisons (5 metrics * 10 pairwise comparisons ≈ 50 tests), which is less conservative than Bonferroni but more robust for this exploratory experimental analysis.",
  "predictive_model_recommendation": "Avoid Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression for predicting Stimulation Paradigm from performance variables because the response variable (Stim Paradigm) is categorical (nominal). Instead, recommend multinomial logistic regression if treating paradeigm as the outcome to be predicted from the metrics, or cluster analysis (k-means) to group performance profiles. However, given the small class sizes for some groups (e.g., Bright Visual Only), a naive Bayes classifier or a k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) model may provide better robustness for classification performance.",
  "assumptions_and_diagnostics": [
    "Normality of residuals checked via Q-Q plots and Shapiro-Wilk test for each metric within each paradigm.",
    "Homogeneity of variances checked via Levene's test; unequal variances observed due to the disparity in sample size (Sham vs Combined) may require Welch's adjustment.",
    "Independence of observations assumed as per randomization procedures in the experimental design.",
    "Check for outliers in Time-to-Target (min 0.5, max 201.4) which is highly skewed and may violate normality; consider log-transformation for Time-to-Target if distributions are non-Gaussian.",
    "For 'Success', verify the binary distribution is not heavily imbalanced within low-N groups before applying standard ANOVA assumptions."
  ],
  "expected_findings": [
    "Sham group is expected to show significantly lower performance scores (worse Time-to-Target, lower Path Efficiency, lower Average Speed) and lower Success rate compared to Combined and ICMS groups.",
    "Dim Visual Only and Bright Visual Only groups are expected to show intermediate performance, potentially clustered with Sham if visual enhancement is insufficient without electrical stimulation.",
    "Combined group is hypothesized to outperform all other individual and control groups in Time-to-Target, Success, and Path Efficiency.",
    "Angular Dispersion (AD) is expected to be highest in Sham (indicating disorientation) and lowest in Combined or ICMS groups (indicating precise landmark usage).",
    "Significant interactions are not applicable here as it is a one-way design, but the main effects are expected to be highly significant.",
    "Large sample sizes (Total n=76655) will provide high statistical power to detect even small effect sizes, driven primarily by the gap between Sham (mean Success ~0.27) and Combined (mean Success ~0.78)."
  ],
  "limitations": [
    "Unequal sample sizes across paradigms (Sham n=3505 vs Combined n=48846), which can lead to Type I error inflation and violate the homogeneity of variance assumption in standard ANOVA.",
    "Skewed distribution of 'Time-to-Target' (Max 201 vs Mean 2.8) may violate the normality assumption of ANOVA, necessitating non-parametric alternatives (Kruskal-Wallis) or transformations.",
    "'Success' is a binary variable; treating it in ANOVA approximates a t-test on proportions but ignores the discrete zero-one structure; logistic regression would be theoretically superior.",
    "Potential confounding by the 'Mouse' variable (8 levels) is hidden in the summary; the detailed ANOVA plan assumes independence unless a mixed-effects model including Mouse as a random intercept is deployed.",
    "Only summary statistics are provided; raw data distribution shapes and specific covariates are not visible here."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Fit a Linear Mixed-Effects Model (LMM) for each performance metric with Stim Paradigm as a fixed effect and Mouse ID as a random intercept to account for repeated measures or inherent mouse-to-mouse variability, addressing the potential confound seen in the categorical summary."
}
